一橋慶喜.note: Tokugawa Yoshinobu (Keiki), head of the Hitotsubashi house and, at this date, Superintendent of the Defense of the Imperial Palace; he became the fifteenth and last shogun in 1866. His personal notice of Kondō marks how high the farmer's son had risen.

上野彦馬.note: A samurai of the Ōmura domain (1838–1904) and a pioneer of photography in Japan, who kept a famous studio at Nagasaki. His portraits of Bakumatsu figures survive; the photograph of Kondō is historical.

松本良順.note: A Dutch-school physician, personal doctor to the shogun Iemochi, who befriended the Shinsengumi and later tended the dying Okita. After the Restoration, as Matsumoto Jun, he became Surgeon-General of the new army and a baron.

ch28.anchor: In Kyoto, no doubt, they called make-up hotogara
ch28.note: Hotogara was a Bakumatsu word for a photographic likeness, and for the sitting that produced it. Toshizō, who has never heard it, takes it for a word for face-paint — which is the joke, for Kondō is indeed painted white: the wet collodion plates of the day were so slow that a sitter had to be powdered with lead-white and backed by white cloth, and to hold stone-still for a long exposure, to register at all.

ch28.anchor: Hitotsubashi Yoshinobu — the future fifteenth shogun
ch28.note: Tokugawa (Hitotsubashi) Yoshinobu, 1837–1913, then Superintendent of the Defense of the Imperial Palace and the strong man of the shogunal party in Kyoto. In 1866 he became the fifteenth and last shogun, and in 1867 surrendered the government to the Emperor. Shiba’s parenthesis looks ahead to that.

Ueno Hikoma (1838–1904), one of the first professional photographers in Japan, who learned the chemistry of the art at Nagasaki from the Dutch naval surgeon Pompe van Meerdervoort (the “Pompe” here) and kept a celebrated studio there. Many of the faces of the Restoration — Sakamoto Ryōma among them — survive only in his plates.

Matsumoto Ryōjun (1832–1907), a leading Dutch-school physician and the shogun’s own doctor, who studied under Pompe at Nagasaki. He grew close to the Shinsengumi in its last years and tended the consumptive Okita. After the Restoration, renamed Jun, he rose to Surgeon-General of the imperial army and was made a baron.

ch28.anchor: an expel-the-barbarian man of the National-Learning school
ch28.note: The National Learning (kokugaku) was the nativist scholarship that sought Japan’s pure origins in its oldest texts and shrines, before any Chinese or Western taint. Its more fervent adherents held a “divine-land” faith that reckoned anything foreign a pollution — even a barbarian’s footprint, even a photograph — which is why Itō’s men will not so much as look at the camera.

The chapter ends on the fact. Yamanami, the learned senior man shelved as general secretary and drawn toward Itō, fled the corps in the second month of Keiō 1 (1865). Under the Code he himself had helped frame, desertion meant death: he was brought back and made to cut his belly, with Okita for his second. He was the most famous man the Code destroyed.
